Editorial: Only You Can Prevent Maine’s Next Dumpster Fire
By: Jon Fetherston

Smokey Bear had a simple message: Only you can prevent wildfires. Here's mine: Only you can prevent Maine's next dumpster fire. Vote Tuesday, Nov. 3.

You've seen the commercials. You've heard the promises. You've probably received enough campaign mail to heat your house for a week. Now these candidates want you to put them in charge of your money. Before you do, ask what they've done to earn your trust.

Are you satisfied with how Augusta spends your money? Do you trust the oversight of nonprofit organizations that receive public funds? When questions about fraud come up, do the people in charge demand answers, or do they get defensive because somebody dared to ask? As a reporter, I expect answers. As a taxpayer, I'm tired of paying for excuses.

The people who depend on legitimate services deserve better, too. Every dollar lost to fraud or waste is a dollar that can't help someone who needs it. If elected officials care about protecting vulnerable people, they should welcome scrutiny of the organizations paid to serve them. Show us where the money went. Show us who received the services. Explain what happens when someone breaks the rules. That is a reasonable expectation when you're spending other people's money.

Instead, taxpayers are too often expected to keep paying and accept another promise that somebody is looking into it. How long are we supposed to wait? We can spend hours arguing about plastic straws. Surely we can bring the same determination to addiction, discarded needles and neighborhood safety. Calling a policy compassionate doesn't answer whether it works.

Families and individuals living with addiction need treatment and a path to recovery. Residents deserve safe streets. Taxpayers deserve to know whether the programs they fund deliver either. The same scrutiny belongs in our schools, our housing policies and every department asking for more money. It belongs on the campaign trail, too.

Troy Jackson wants your vote. What in his record convinces you he has earned it? What has he accomplished that makes your life better? If your strongest argument for voting for him is that you hate Donald Trump, think about what that gets you after Election Day. Anger at the "Orange Man" won't pay your property taxes or improve your child's school. Is Susan Collins as conservative as me? Nope. Is she what Maine is all about? Absolutely!

Hannah Pingree should face the same questions. If you're dissatisfied with Gov. Janet Mills' leadership, what convinces you Pingree would deliver a better result? What would she change? Voters deserve more than a familiar name and another round of promises.

I support Bobby Charles because I believe he offers a better chance to bring accountability to Augusta. If he wins, I'll expect him to deliver. I'll ask where the money went, whether his policies are working and whether he's keeping his word. Having an "R" next to his name won't buy him a pass.

Pay attention to the legislative races, too. Maine lawmakers choose the secretary of state. If you don't want Shenna Bellows returned to that office, the people you send to Augusta matter. These are jobs you pay for. Examine the applicants accordingly. Read their records, question their promises and consider whether your family can afford what they're proposing.

Then show up. If you're unhappy with the direction of Maine, staying home leaves the decision to everyone else. Complaining on Wednesday won't make up for sitting out Tuesday. And if you keep rewarding failure, why would you expect anything to change?

Only you can prevent the next dumpster fire. Vote Tuesday.

My son was spotted by a MIT admissions person for his building a remote-controlled hover craft from parts he took from his R/C toys (he was 11 at the time) along with using cardboard and a trash bag. That thing was so cool. The admission person did tell me he would have an incredibly difficult time getting in because he was male and white. 

One thing led to another, and he was contacted by a MIT ambassador. The ambassador thought he would have zero issues getting in based on academics and accomplishments (he had a lot by 14). He had a perfect SAT Math score. He was told again white males were the lowest number of students offered acceptance. 

In the end he decided to not pursue MIT and went to RPI in Troy NY. Now at 28 he is the lead kinetic hardware engineer at a defense company. You know, the part that goes BOOM. His talent is what got him to where he is not the schools name on the diploma.

text:
Content warning: this post discusses the murder of a 13 year old girl.

On this day, Friday, October 31, 1913, 113 years ago, Judge Leonard Strickland Roan approved the brief of evidence in the Leo Max Frank case as "true, correct and complete." These three pages are part of that brief.

Slide 0726, Slide 0727 and Slide 0728, from Leo Frank's appeal records at the Georgia Supreme Court, show Defendant's Exhibit 4a. The typed heading calls them "Packing room reports, being part of data for financial."

Mary Anne Phagan was murdered at the National Pencil Company on Saturday, April 26, 1913. Frank, the factory superintendent, was convicted of her murder on August 25, 1913.

The financial sheet was the heart of Frank's alibi for that Saturday afternoon. He told the jury he made it out every Saturday afternoon, "as has been my custom," and that he was hard at work on it in his office.

These slips are the raw material he said he worked from. Each is a printed National Pencil Company "Daily Report" for the packing department, Department No. 13, filled in by hand and signed "Eula."

In his statement Frank named her as Miss Eula May Flowers, the forelady of the packing department. The reports run from Friday, April 18, to Thursday, April 24, 1913, the last day of the factory's fiscal week.

Each line is a pencil number, a brand and the gross packed that day. The brands read like a catalog of 1913: Oxford, Trumps, Packard, Cadillac, Genius, Emblem, Sitting Bull, Khedive, G. Wash and J. Monroe.

Now listen to what Frank said about them. "Mr. Schiff had entered the production for April 18, 19, 22 and 23, but he had omitted the entry for the 24," he told the jury, as The Atlanta Journal printed it on August 19, 1913.

So by his own account, the packing entries left for him that afternoon were Thursday's. Look at Slide 0728, from Leo Frank's appeal records at the Georgia Supreme Court.

Thursday, April 24, is two small forms. Between them they hold about a dozen lines of figures, already added up by the forelady: 153, 136 and 54, with a total of 343.

Frank said the Thursday report was handed in by Miss Flowers on Friday. He called the work of going through such data "not a hard job, but a very tedious one."

Think about that for a moment. The defense offered these slips to show how much work filled Frank's afternoon, and the slips show how little of it was left.

Frank described other tasks too: the job sheet, a repack slip, the payroll and the invoices. Even there, he admitted he worked one average price only "approximately," and that he let part of the work go, "intending to put that in on Monday."

The state never accepted the financial sheet as an alibi. Hattie Hall, a stenographer, told the coroner's inquest, "I remember the previous Saturday I was at the pencil factory and I helped him make up the financial sheet."

She also said, "I don't work on Saturday afternoons." Her inquest words are State's Exhibit 2, Slide 0720, from Leo Frank's appeal records at the Georgia Supreme Court.

In his closing argument, Solicitor General Hugh Manson Dorsey told the jury that Frank "did not do any work on the financial sheet after Saturday at noon," as The Atlanta Georgian reported on August 24, 1913.

Dorsey's point was plain. "If he could go home into the bosom of his family after such an atrocious crime, he could have made that sheet."

The jury heard the slips, the sheet and the man, and convicted him. Judge Roan approved this record on October 31, 1913, and the Georgia Supreme Court affirmed the conviction on February 17, 1914.

The bottom half of Slide 0728, from Leo Frank's appeal records at the Georgia Supreme Court, begins Defendant's Exhibit 4b, the job department reports. They are signed by the job department forelady, whom Frank named as Miss Fannie Atherton.

Forever 13 and Never forgotten.

#MaryPhagan #LeoFrank

text: 53/100 A small number next to a photo can feel like a verdict on your worth. In a 2016 study, Lauren Sherman and colleagues at UCLA scanned the brains of teenagers while they viewed photos in a mock Instagram feed. Photos shown with many likes activated reward-related regions more strongly, including the nucleus accumbens. Teens were also more likely to like photos that already had many likes, even when the photos showed risky behaviour. The sample was small, about thirty teens, and lab feeds differ from real ones. Other research on social media and well-being has produced mixed results. Large analyses by Amy Orben and Andrew Przybylski found small average links between screen time and adolescent well-being. Yet some groups and some patterns of use seem more affected than others. The likes study still offers a sharp picture of overvaluation in miniature. A post becomes a test. The count becomes a score. The brain's reward system treats the score as meaningful, so checking becomes compulsive. Each refresh is a small act of gripping. December amplifies this, with year-end photo dumps and holiday posts competing for attention. Noticing the grip is a start. Posting something and then putting the phone away for an hour is a cheap experiment in letting go of a verdict nobody actually needs.

🇺🇸 #G20 Sidelines | 🇫🇷 🇸🇦 | France, Saudi Arabia and the Gulf: Strategic Autonomy Beyond Washington

The frequency of Saudi-French ministerial contacts, with meetings in Riyadh on October 19 and again in Atlanta today, October 31, reflects sustained diplomatic coordination amid growing regional security challenges. More broadly, it illustrates France’s ambition to strengthen its independent strategic position in the Gulf without necessarily displacing or confronting the United States.

Paris is seeking to expand its role as a security and diplomatic partner for Gulf countries, particularly Saudi Arabia, while encouraging greater diversification of defence and international partnerships. For France, this means maintaining the capacity to act alongside Washington when interests converge, but also preserving diplomatic and operational independence when they do not.

The Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb are central to this approach. Their security affects energy supplies, international trade and global supply chains. France has therefore sought to distinguish its support for maritime security and freedom of navigation from automatic participation in US-led military operations. Its preference for an international framework reflects an effort to retain diplomatic flexibility and build broader international support.

Saudi Arabia has its own reasons for pursuing this relationship. Riyadh is diversifying its strategic partnerships, seeking to strengthen its diplomatic leverage and avoid excessive dependence on any single external security provider. France offers an additional channel for defence cooperation, diplomatic coordination and engagement with Europe.

This does not mean France is attempting to replace the United States or that Saudi Arabia is turning away from Washington. American military capabilities remain central to Gulf security. Rather, Paris is pursuing strategic autonomy, while Riyadh is pursuing strategic diversification.

The broader geopolitical significance is that Gulf security is increasingly becoming a field of overlapping partnerships rather than an exclusively American-led framework. France wants a greater role in shaping that environment, Saudi Arabia wants more room for manoeuvre, and Washington remains a central actor with whom both countries must coordinate.

The underlying issue is not whether France can bypass the United States, but whether it can become an indispensable diplomatic and security partner in a region where American leadership is no longer the only channel through which regional governments seek to protect their interests.

text:
🇺🇸 Economic Security Begins at Sea: Rubio’s Message to the G20

At today’s G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting, @SecRubio underscored a fundamental connection between maritime security, food security and economic stability. His message reflects a broader understanding of economic security: the resilience of national economies depends not only on domestic policies and financial systems, but also on the security of the international networks that sustain global trade.

Maritime routes are the arteries of the global economy. Major shipping corridors, strategic waterways and port infrastructure underpin the movement of energy, agricultural products and essential goods. Disruptions to these routes, whether through armed conflict, attacks on commercial vessels or restrictions on navigation, can have consequences far beyond the immediate region, driving up transportation and insurance costs, disrupting supply chains and increasing economic uncertainty.

Food security is equally strategic. It depends not simply on agricultural production, but on reliable access to fertilisers, energy, transportation and international markets. Disruptions to these interconnected systems can expose import-dependent countries to price shocks, supply shortages and geopolitical pressure.

Taken together, these vulnerabilities illustrate how economic interdependence can become a source of strategic exposure. Control over maritime access, the movement of essential commodities and the reliability of supply chains can translate into significant geopolitical leverage.

The broader implication is that economic security can no longer be treated as separate from national and international security. For the G20, the challenge is to move beyond recognising these interdependencies and strengthen cooperation to protect maritime corridors, maintain open trade routes and build more resilient food and supply systems.

In today’s geopolitical environment, securing the arteries of global commerce is not merely a matter of trade policy. It is an essential dimension of economic resilience, national security and international stability.

text:
On 30 October, Reuters reported that Pentagon officials had asked several European allies to tone down their warnings about Russia. The ones named were Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, and the message was delivered in private meetings over recent weeks. The policy chief, Elbridge Colby, is reported to have urged a Baltic official not to "poke" Russia, and to have pointed to talk of Russia being "cornered like a rat" as unhelpful. The reasoning, as reported, was that some European statements could undermine security on the continent. A European official put the advice in four words: "Don't make noise." Washington has not confirmed any of this, and Tallinn says nothing reached it through official channels, so I hold it as reported and no more.

Even so, it is worth asking what the request would mean if it is true, because it does not stand alone. In my earlier essay on balance we followed a pattern from September to October: Kyiv told to stop striking Russian diesel, then a deal to bring Russian diesel to market. Now the countries nearest to Russia, the ones with the most to lose and the least room to be wrong, are reportedly asked to speak more softly. That is the same direction a third time, and a pattern needs more than one point before it is worth naming.

What a balancer would want

George Friedman's account of American strategy gives the plainest explanation, and I take it as that: Washington does not want a Eurasia that coordinates against it, and it does not want a Russia pushed so hard that it has nowhere to go but Beijing. Quiet in the Baltics serves both. It lowers the temperature that might pull American forces deeper into Europe, and it fits with the review of troop levels that the reports tie to Colby, who wants Europeans to carry more of their own defense so that American attention can turn to the Pacific. None of this needs sympathy for Moscow. It is what a sea power does when it wants to choose its wars.

The honest counter-reading belongs here at full strength. Some Western officials, the reports say, genuinely believe that loud talk plays into the Kremlin's hands, and the case is not foolish: words can harden an adversary, and a frightened Russia is more dangerous than a confident one. Europeans also have a duty to tell their own voters the truth. Both things can be so at once, and the request may be exactly what it says it is, a plea for prudence.

Where the test falls

So I do not ask whether the request is wicked. I ask what else the same hand is doing, since the matter turns on the whole direction and not on one phone call. Earlier I set out several things to watch: pressure on the size and alignment of Ukraine's postwar army, resistance to European-led guarantees, softness on Russian trade. This week adds one more thing to watch. If Washington is balancing, we should see quiet asked of the exposed states together with continued reassurance and presence for them. If instead quiet comes with a thinning of presence, the request is no longer prudence, it is a withdrawal with a polite voice. The reports mention the troop review and sanctions relief held out to Russia, and nothing yet shows which way it falls. I would call this one open, and I would not move any odds on it.

What Scripture says about warning

Here the essay leaves strategy, because Scripture has a good deal to say about the one who is told to stay quiet. Isaiah gave us the reversal in the earlier essay, and the form this week is mild but recognizable: the nation that sounds the alarm is the one asked to lower its voice.

Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness, who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter! (Isaiah 5:20, ESV)

I do not say the Baltic states are prophets or that Russia is the beast. States are named here, persons are not, and a warning can be wrong. What I say is that Ezekiel gives the watchman a rule that does not bend to diplomacy:

But if the watchman sees the sword coming and does not blow the trumpet, so that the people are not warned, and the sword comes and takes any one of them, that person is taken away in his iniquity, but his blood I will require at the watchman's hand. (Ezekiel 33:6, ESV)

A watchman is judged on whether he blew the trumpet when he saw the sword, not on whether the trumpet was convenient for the king's negotiations. That cuts in two directions, and we must say both. If the Baltic intelligence services really judge a test of NATO's mutual defense unlikely, as one European official is quoted as saying, then a loud alarm would be a false trumpet, and false trumpets cost the real ones their hearing. But if the sword is visible, the instruction to be quiet is a request to fail at the one task a watchman has.

Paul adds a warning about what the quiet tends to say:

Now concerning the times and the seasons, brothers, you have no need to have anything written to you. For you yourselves are fully aware that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. While people are saying, “There is peace and security,” then sudden destruction will come upon them as labor pains come upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape. (1 Thessalonians 5:1-3, ESV)

This is the fifth category of the Wildcard's watching, peace and safety against the backdrop of real escalation, and the sign is the gap between the declaration and the structure. This week the declaration is "keep calm," and the structure is the same as before: Russian sabotage in Europe is reported as continuing, and Russia has not changed its aims. The gap is small, it may close, and it is not a countdown. Paul's own point is that the day does not come by calculation, and we are told to be sober and awake, not to name a date.

And the proverb is worth a thought:

A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet. (Proverbs 29:5, ESV)

It does not accuse anyone. It describes what soft words can do to the one who hears them, and it fits the case of a Europe being reassured by a patron that is also offering the other side sanctions relief.

The Kittim, once more

If the United States is the Kittim of Daniel 11:30, as I read it, then Daniel's picture is of a sea power whose arrival turns a king back, and what follows is the king's fear, rage and turn against the covenant. Earlier we kept Kyiv at the first seal and kept the covenant action for later. This essay changes none of that. It adds only that the Kittim's power is exercised in two ways, by ships and by speech, and that the reported request is of the second kind. Rome in 168 BC drew a circle in the sand and told Antiochus to answer before he left it. Washington reportedly tells its friends to speak low. They are not the same act. Rome gave an ultimatum to the aggressor, and this is a request to the exposed, which is why the word "inversion" has to be used with care and with the evidence of the next weeks, not of this one.

What I hold, and what I leave open

The reported request fits the balancing reading and does not prove it. It fits the Isaiah pattern and does not prove that either. I hold three things. The order of Scripture I read from the text. That balance explains this request is my reading, and this one thing to watch can prove me wrong: if presence in the Baltics is reinforced as the voices are lowered, prudence is the better word. That the exposed are asked to be quiet while the aggressor is offered relief is a fact, if the reports stand, and it belongs on the record whatever it turns out to mean.

The call on us does not wait for the answer. Ezekiel's watchman blows the trumpet when he sees the sword, and Paul's brothers are told to stay awake and sober. May God give us the discernment to tell a true alarm from a false one, the courage not to be hushed when the sword is real, and the humility to be corrected when it is not; and to the Lamb who conquers be all glory.

🇷🇺⚔️🇺🇦 Patriot Deal Leaves Kiev Waiting Until 2030 as $2.1bn Air-Defence Promise Collides With Reality

WASHINGTON — A newly approved $2.1 billion US sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 MSE interceptor missiles to Ukraine is being presented as a major boost to Kiev’s air defences, but the headline figure disguises an uncomfortable reality: the missiles are not expected to begin arriving until around 2030.

The US State Department approved the possible Foreign Military Sale on October 30, with Lockheed Martin named as principal contractor. Reuters reports the interceptors still have to be manufactured, while production backlogs and competing global orders could leave Ukraine waiting into the early 2030s.

That timetable offers little comfort to Vladimir Zelensky, who says Kiev urgently needs far more Patriot interceptors during the winter of 2026–27. Zelensky says Ukraine has received only about 12 Patriot missiles a month from the United States this year, while Russian attacks have placed sustained pressure on the country’s air-defence network.

Kiev has asked Washington for a winter package of roughly 100 Patriot interceptors a month. Zelensky is now pressing the United States and European allies to release missiles from existing military stockpiles immediately, with the newly ordered weapons used to replenish those arsenals years later.

The proposal exposes the central weakness of the $2.1 billion announcement. Politically, Washington can point to a dramatic package of 500 advanced interceptors. Militarily, however, missiles arriving after 2030 cannot defend power stations, heating infrastructure or cities during the coming winter.

Production constraints are severe. Industry analysts say the PAC-3 MSE manufacturing cycle can take around two years, while Lockheed Martin is trying to expand output amid surging demand from US allies.

There is also disagreement over the wider supply picture. NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, said this week that paid-for packages under the PURL mechanism had not been delayed and that deliveries were continuing.

Even so, Kiev’s problem remains immediate. A multi-billion-dollar weapons approval may sound decisive, but without accelerated transfers from existing Western stockpiles, the deal risks becoming another example of military aid announced today but delivered long after the crisis that justified it.

WORLD NEWS REPORT — OCTOBER 31, 2026
Global Edition | Politics, War, Economy, Technology, Health, Climate and World Affairs
UNITED STATES — ELECTIONS ENTER CRITICAL FINAL DAYS
Americans are approaching the November 3 midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress. Republicans currently hold narrow congressional majorities, while Democrats seek to regain legislative power. More than 51 million Americans have already voted.
Legal confrontations are intensifying. A federal judge ordered the Trump administration to stop threatening election officials with prosecution over disputed voter-registration demands. In California and Alaska, litigation involving voter eligibility and election procedures continues. Officials emphasize the importance of lawful voting and public confidence in election results.

Reuters+1
GLOBAL DIPLOMACY — G20 MEETING ENDS WITHOUT AGREEMENT

Foreign ministers from major economies concluded their Atlanta meeting without a joint declaration. Disagreements involved Ukraine, Iran, international trade and relations with Russia.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged that solutions remain distant. European representatives objected to Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov's participation. Negotiators nevertheless discussed energy security, critical minerals and international supply chains. The next major diplomatic test comes at December's G20 leaders' summit in Florida.

AP News
UKRAINE — LIMITED CEASEFIRE PROPOSAL EMERGES

Russia's full-scale invasion, launched February 24, 2022, remains unresolved. The United States and Canada report increasing interest in a limited Black Sea ceasefire protecting grain and energy shipments.
Turkey and India have advanced proposals. Such an arrangement could protect international commerce without ending the wider war. Washington has also approved a proposed $2.1 billion sale of Patriot air-defense interceptors to Ukraine. Moscow and Kyiv remain divided over security guarantees, territory and future military arrangements. No comprehensive peace agreement has been reached.

Reuters+1
MIDDLE EAST — IRAN CONFLICT THREATENS GLOBAL ENERGY

Tensions surrounding the United States, Israel and Iran remain severe following military conflict that began earlier this year.
Iranian Revolutionary Guards reported multiple tanker fires in the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters could not independently verify all Iranian claims. Maritime authorities separately reported attacks involving commercial vessels.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan and Qatar have pursued diplomatic efforts to prevent another escalation. Further disruption in the strategically important strait could increase worldwide energy and transportation costs.

Reuters+1
ECONOMY — STRONG GROWTH MEETS PERSISTENT INFLATION

The American economy expanded at a 3.4% annualized rate during the third quarter. Consumer spending rose 3.8%, while business-equipment investment increased sharply.
Yet September's personal consumption expenditures inflation reached 3.6%, significantly exceeding the Federal Reserve's 2% objective.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh faces a difficult balancing act: restraining prices without unnecessarily weakening economic growth. Higher fuel costs, borrowing expenses and energy bills remain important financial pressures for households.

Reuters+1
TECHNOLOGY — AI INVESTMENT FACES GROWING SCRUTINY

Technology markets are reassessing enormous artificial-intelligence investments amid questions about profitability and infrastructure costs.
Reuters reported that OpenAI reduced its fundraising target by $10 billion, citing a Financial Times report. Investor attention is also shifting toward the long-term financial commitments of major AI developers.

Artificial intelligence continues transforming research, software and business operations. Whether revenues can justify extraordinary computing expenditures remains a central unresolved question.

Reuters+1
GLOBAL HEALTH — INFECTIOUS DISEASE WARNINGS

The United States reported 4,852 measles cases as of October 29, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The increase underscores continuing concerns about vaccination coverage and preventable transmission.
Bangladesh is experiencing a serious dengue outbreak, with hundreds of reported deaths during 2026. Nigerian authorities have also reported two suspected Ebola cases; suspicion does not establish laboratory confirmation.

Public-health agencies continue emphasizing surveillance, vaccination where available and rapid outbreak investigation.

Reuters+2
ENVIRONMENT — BIODIVERSITY AGREEMENT REACHED

Countries participating in COP17 reached an agreement intended to accelerate protection of biodiversity.
However, financing remains insufficient to meet conservation ambitions. Scientists and environmental organizations continue warning that habitat destruction, species loss and climate pressures threaten food systems, water supplies and economic stability.

The central challenge is translating international commitments into measurable protection supported by sustained funding.

Reuters
AFRICA — DIPLOMATIC TRANSITION AND OLYMPIC HISTORY

The United Nations has closed its political mission in Somalia, ending approximately three decades of direct political engagement. Somalia continues confronting difficult security and governance challenges.
Meanwhile, Senegal is preparing to host Africa's first Youth Olympic Games, marking an important milestone for international sport and the continent's growing role in global athletics.

Al Jazeera+1
CONCLUSION — A WORLD AT A TURNING POINT

October 31 reveals three defining international challenges: preventing military escalation, preserving confidence in democratic institutions and managing economic transformation.
Diplomatic proposals offer possibilities rather than guaranteed settlements. Artificial intelligence presents opportunity alongside financial uncertainty. Public-health and environmental challenges require sustained international cooperation.

The immediate developments to watch are America's November 3 elections, possible renewed Middle Eastern hostilities, negotiations over Ukrainian shipping security and central-bank decisions responding to persistent inflation.

The overriding finding: global stability increasingly depends on whether governments can turn competing national interests into practical agreements before existing crises deepen.

text: Ukraine did pause the refinery strikes for about two weeks after Washington pushed, and Russian refineries raised output during the halt. The strikes came back Friday as Russia kept bombing Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Rosneft told Bloomberg the losses are becoming unsustainable, and Russia is the world's second largest diesel supplier. Zelensky has also offered to stop the oil strikes in exchange for Patriot missiles.
